title: Arjuna Sees Only the Bird
hookLine: Drona asks his students what they see, and only Arjuna sees just the bird: Vaisheshika's mind, one gate at a time
carry: the mind is one gate; the self is the knower
tomorrow: why does a flame always rise? Vaisheshika's answer goes back to dharma.
last: MEET THE PERSON, NOT THE KICK.

cards: Drona, teacher of the Kuru princes, has a wooden bird set high in a tree. One by one he calls his students up, bows drawn. What do you see?
Yudhishthira says: the tree, the bird, you, my brothers. Step aside, says Drona. The others say much the same.
Then Arjuna. What do you see? Only the bird.
Describe it. I see its head, nothing else. Shoot, says Drona.

teach.b: That's the Mahabharata; popular retellings make it the bird's eye. Vaisheshika gives you a way to see what happened. Its first category, substance, comes in nine kinds.
Earth, water, fire, air: the four kinds of atom. Then akasha, the space that carries sound. Then time and direction.

teach.h: BREATH IS A SIGN OF THE SELF.
teach.b: And last, two that aren't stuff at all: the self, atman, and the mind, manas. How do you know there's a self? The Sutra lists its marks, and the first is breathing out and breathing in.
Then the eyelids opening and closing, life itself, and further on, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion and effort.

teach.h: THE MIND: ONE THING AT A TIME.
teach.b: And the mind? Sometimes, the Sutra notes, self, senses and object are all in contact, and still no knowing happens. You stare at a page and take nothing in.
Something has to be the gate, and that gate is manas. In this school it's tiny, so it joins one sense at a time. On this view, nobody truly reads and listens at once; the mind only switches, fast.

Read Arjuna that way: his eyes took in the whole tree like everyone's, but his mind let in only the bird. Hindu practice prizes that one-pointed mind, ekagrata, and trains it with one bead, one name, one flame.

Behind the gate is the self, the knower. So the week closes: Gargi's honest questions, the voice that only sounded like Rama, Nachiketa's doubt, the gleaner's handful, the seed, Bhrigu's kick, and now the bird.
At a desk with three screens open, the old school's line holds: one gate, one thing.

how: Students of Vaisheshika learn the nine substances, from earth to mind, and the Nyaya-Vaisheshika tradition uses the self's marks to argue that the self is real; in Hindu practice, japa on a mala, one bead and one name at a time, trains the same one-pointed mind.

o: a daily rite of sweeping and cleaning the home
a school that charts the stars and the planets
the school whose list ends with the self and the mind

games.q: the end of the list — tap the pairs.
p: the self, known by its marks
the mind, a gate for one thing
the first mark of the self

s: Yudhishthira passed Drona's test by seeing everything
he saw the tree, the teacher and his brothers, and Drona told him to step aside.
in Vaisheshika, the mind can take in two senses at once
the mind is tiny and joins one sense at a time; we only switch fast.
the self and the mind are on Vaisheshika's list of substances
the nine substances end with atman and manas.

games.q: you're doing homework with a show on and your phone buzzing. by Vaisheshika and Arjuna's test, what's happening?
o: you're taking in all three at once.
the mind, one gate, is switching fast between them.
the eyes and ears decide, so the mind isn't involved.
games.why: the Sutra says self, senses and object can all be in contact and still no knowing happens. the mind joins one sense at a time, which is how Arjuna saw only the bird.

practice: Take a mala if you have one, or just use your fingers. With each bead or each finger, say one name of God, Om, Ram, Shiva, whichever is yours. If you don't pray, count one breath.
One bead, one name. When a sound pulls you away, that's the gate swinging; swing it back. Like Arjuna: only the bird.

wordCard.voice: Vaisheshika. Its nine substances end with the self, known by signs like breathing, and the mind, a gate that lets in one thing at a time.

orig.note: Sanskrit: manas, the mind; in Vaisheshika, a substance that joins one sense at a time.
